summary: This Standards Track document defines a YANG data model for policy-based network access control by group identity, extending ACLs with date and time parameters for schedule-aware enforcement. It also defines a RADIUS extension for when access is triggered by user authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: Rules say who can go where, and when, such as letting a group into a room only during certain hours.

questions: what is the user-access-group-id radius attribute
how do acls match on group id
subtitle: Write network access rules for groups of users, devices or applications, switch them on by schedule, and hand out the group ID through RADIUS.

tldr.problem: Endpoints move and change IP addresses, and the same people may need different network access at different times. Rules written per IP address are hard to keep correct.
tldr.mechanism: A YANG module extends the ACL model of RFC 8519 so that rules match on source and destination endpoint group IDs and can carry a date and time schedule. A new RADIUS attribute, User-Access-Group-ID, tells the network access server which group a user belongs to.
tldr.outcome: Policies can follow groups instead of addresses, but the document leaves the mapping from a group ID to packet fields to the deployment, and some devices may need hardware or software upgrades.

today: RFC 10065 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2026, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the ACL model of RFC 8519 and the scheduling model of RFC 9922.

sections.title: Why Group-Based Access Control
sections.content:
Remote access, VPNs and Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) policies give employees flexibility, but they also raise risk. RFC 10065 names two problems. First, endpoints do not have stable and unique IP addresses: WLAN and VPN clients move, VM-based servers move, and mechanisms such as IPv6 temporary addresses and NAPT add more instability. That makes policies built on the 5-tuple hard to enforce consistently.

Second, the same endpoints may need different security policies in different circumstances. Access might depend on location, source network reputation, role, time of day, device type or a device's security posture.

The document answers with a YANG data model that extends the Access Control List (ACL) module of RFC 8519 so that policy follows a group identity, plus a RADIUS attribute that carries the user group identifier. It does not say how a group ID is mapped to dedicated packet fields. Group-Based Policy, discussed in RFC 9638, is given as one example of how that may be done.

MAC addresses appear as an example identifier, but the RFC says these examples are not recommendations: MAC-based ACLs can be bypassed by clearing the MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: Kids keep changing seats, so a rule that says 'the kid in seat 5' keeps breaking. A rule about 'the red team' keeps working wherever they sit.

sections.title: The Architecture and Its Five Steps
sections.content:
The example architecture has a service orchestrator, an SDN controller that acts as the Policy Decision Point (PDP), a Network Access Server (NAS), an AAA server and one or more Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs). The controller keeps the endpoint-group-based ACLs and the mapping from a group to packet header fields, and pushes policy to the PEPs. A PEP exposes a YANG-based interface, for example NETCONF, to the controller.

The typical flow has five steps:

  • Step 1: administrators or the orchestrator configure the SDN controller with network-level ACLs using the new YANG module.
  • Step 2: a user logging on is authenticated at the NAS.
  • Step 3: the NAS relays the request to the AAA server, for example with RADIUS. On success, the group identifier comes back to the NAS. On failure, the user gets no group (an Access-Reject) or a special group with very limited access, depending on local policy.
  • Step 4: either the AAA server or the NAS tells the controller how the group ID maps to packet header attributes such as the 5-tuple. How this notification is done is out of scope.
  • Step 5: the PEPs hold either group-based ACLs or ACLs based on packet header fields. Both kinds may exist on one PEP.

For device or application groups, the mapping is kept on the controller from an inventory or an application registry, so RADIUS exchanges are not required.
sections.plainLanguage: A visitor shows an ID at the front desk. The desk asks the office which team the visitor is on, and then tells the door guards to apply that team's rules.

sections.title: Endpoint Groups
sections.content:
An endpoint is an end user, an enterprise device or an application that connects to a network. An endpoint group is a set of endpoints that share common access control policies, and an endpoint group identifier represents its collective identity. There are three kinds:

  • User group: users assigned the same network access policy. Membership is decided by predefined criteria such as source IP address, geolocation, time of day or device certificate, and a user can move to another group when those attributes change.
  • Device group: enterprise devices that share policies. Matching a group ID instead of addresses shields policy from address changes such as a VM-based server migrating.
  • Application group: applications that share policies. One application may run on many devices, VMs or containers, and the policy does not depend on the 5-tuple.

Group criteria are not mutually exclusive. The RFC's own examples include a user group called R&D Regular with ID foo-10 and R&D BYOD with ID foo-11, which differ only in whether clients are corporate-issued or personal. These are illustrations, and the document makes no assumption about how groups are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: There are teams of people, teams of machines and teams of apps. Each team has a name tag, and the rules are written for the name tag.

sections.title: The ietf-ucl-acl YANG Module
sections.content:
The User-group-based Control List (UCL) module, named ietf-ucl-acl, augments the ietf-access-control-list module of RFC 8519 in three places.

  • An endpoint-groups container holds an endpoint-group list. Each entry has a group-id, a string of length 1 to 64, and an optional group-type that can be user-group, device-group or application-group. A string is used rather than an integer so a domain can build a hierarchy of identifiers.
  • An endpoint-group container under matches adds source-group-id and destination-group-id as match criteria. It is valid only when the ACL type is or derives from group-acl-type.
  • An effective-schedule container on each ACE chooses between a period and a recurrence, reusing groupings from the scheduling module of RFC 9922. If no schedule is configured, the ACE is immediately and always applied.

The module also defines features so that implementations can say what they support, and mixed ACL types that combine group matching with Ethernet, IPv4 or IPv6 header matching. Appendix A shows an example: permit R&D BYOD traffic to R&D devices on work days from 8:00:00 to 18:00:00 UTC starting on January 1, 2026, and deny R&D BYOD traffic to finance servers for a fixed period in 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: It adds two things to the rule book: a place to write 'from this team to that team', and a clock that says when the rule is switched on.

sections.title: The User-Access-Group-ID RADIUS Attribute
sections.content:
The User-Access-Group-ID attribute is for cases where network access is triggered by user authentication. It is defined following RFC 6929, has Type 241.12 and the data type string from RFC 8044, and its value is the user group ID.

It MAY appear in an Access-Accept, and when it does the system applies the related access control after the user authenticates. Several instances in one Access-Accept mean the user belongs to many groups. It MAY appear in an Access-Request as a hint of preference, which the server is not required to honor. It MAY also appear in a CoA-Request, and in an Accounting-Request, where a NAS can use it to show it received the attribute and is enforcing the policy. It MUST NOT appear in any other RADIUS packet.

The total Length is at least 4 octets and at most 67 octets, which fits a group ID of up to 64 octets plus one octet each for Type, Length and Extended-Type.
sections.plainLanguage: When the office says yes to a visitor, it also sticks a team sticker on the visitor. The sticker is short, at most 64 letters.

sections.title: Deployment Options and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The model can be deployed in two broad ways. At the network or administrative domain level, the SDN controller keeps the dynamic mapping from a group ID to IP and transport fields and programs the PEPs with address-based or 5-tuple-based ACLs. Then PEPs need no special logic compared with conventional ACLs.

At the device level, the PEP understands group IDs itself. That removes the need for the controller to update PEPs whenever a user's context or a VM changes, but dedicated hardware or software support might be needed. When the NAS is the PEP and gets the group ID from the AAA server without it being carried in packet headers, forwarding performance might be affected. Some devices may need hardware or software upgrades to enforce group-based matches.

The RFC also requires an adequate setup to map group IDs to packet fields, typically managed by a controller, and asks for special care so the mapping stays consistent when several mechanisms, RADIUS among them, are in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Either a central office does the translating and the guards stay simple, or every guard learns to read the team badges. The second way is smoother later but costs more to set up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The YANG module is meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. These have to use a secure transport (the text names SSH, TLS and QUIC) and mutual authentication, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) can limit which users may do what. All writable nodes may be sensitive. Unauthorized writes to the endpoint-group list could forge or delete a group. Writes to the group IDs in an ACE could permit access that should not be permitted or deny access that should be permitted. Writes to effective-schedule could cause disruption. Reading effective-schedule would also let an attacker learn which rules apply and craft an attack.

For RADIUS, the RFC points to RFC 2865 and targets deployments with a trusted relationship between client and server, optionally secured by IPsec or TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could edit the team list or the clock, they could let the wrong people in. So only trusted people, over a locked line, may change it.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content: IANA has assigned the XML namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ucl-acl and registered the YANG module ietf-ucl-acl with prefix ucl. In the RADIUS Attribute Types registry it has assigned value 241.12 to User-Access-Group-ID, with data type string.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list keeper wrote down the new module name and the new sticker number so nobody else uses them.
